title: Amora: Communication-Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
comment: Accepted at SIGMOD 2027
summary: Approximate nearest neighbors search (ANNS) over cloud-hosted vector databases raises a critical privacy concern: the query vector, which often encodes sensitive user intent, is exposed to the server. Private ANNS (PANNS) allows a client to retrieve nearest neighbors without revealing its query. The state-of-the-art single-server scheme, Pacmann (ICLR'25), achieves high accuracy via graph-based search with private information retrieval (PIR), but incurs substantial communication overhead because each PIR query retrieves only a single vertex. We present Amora, a communication-efficient PANNS system that applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index so that one PIR query is amortized over many vertices. To retrieve as much of the distance and neighbor information the search needs under a limited communication budget, Amora adopts a dual-PIR split layout with two heterogeneous PIR matrices that stay balanced in dimension: VecPIR retrieves inner products for an entire partition of vertices as their distance at once, while NbrPIR retrieves necessary neighbor lists at subgroup granularity for graph traversal. This layout shifts the cost model of PIR query from per-vertex to per-partition, which significantly reduces the communication overhead. To further improve efficiency by reducing the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database, Amora introduces batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication, centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions, and TopCand exploration that seeds jump-style graph navigation with the closest vertices from each retrieved partition. We evaluate Amora on five datasets spanning 96 to 1024 dimensions and up to 10 million vectors. Compared to Pacmann, Amora reduces online communication by 93--99% while achieving higher search accuracy.

title: AdaBool: Sparse Boolean Matrix Processing with Adaptive Data Representation
comment: Accepted to ACM SIGMOD 2027 (Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data). 16 pages, 21 figures, 7 tables
summary:
Many data processing tasks revolve around determining whether logical relationships exist between two sets of entities, a pattern that can be naturally modeled as Sparse Boolean Matrix Multiplication (SpBMM). Under Boolean semantics, matrix representations no longer need to store numerical values and instead focus on encoding the positions of non-zero elements, making it highly amenable to data compression for substantially lower memory access overhead. The key challenge, however, is that the most effective compression depends heavily on sparsity distribution: different methods perform best at different sparsity levels, while real-world matrices often contain sharply varying sparsity across regions. Consequently, forcing the entire matrix into any fixed, monolithic representation leaves considerable optimization opportunities untapped.
  We present AdaBool, a SpBMM framework designed to reconcile this tension through an adaptive data representation. AdaBool partitions matrices into fine-grained element blocks and represents each block with the encoding best matched to its local sparsity. On top of this adaptive encoding, AdaBool introduces a heterogeneous GPU execution model that groups blocks by encoding type and maps them to matching processing paths, enabling efficient execution and scheduling across GPU resources. We implement AdaBool end to end with low-level system optimizations, evaluate it on both production and public workloads, and show that it outperforms representative baselines by over an order of magnitude.

title: ConStore: Search-Overlapped Prefetch and Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Storage for Disk-Based ANNS
summary:
Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search, recommendation, and advertising over corpora that exceed memory capacity. Existing ANNS research often focuses on vector search at small top-K, whereas industrial-scale applications require larger retrieval sets. Fetching the corresponding content from storage remains comparatively underexplored. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector corpora shows that, at large K, content fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency and cannot be ignored in end-to-end retrieval.
  We present ConStore, a content storage engine combining two complementary techniques to reduce end-to-end retrieval latency. Speculative Inline Content Prefetch (SICP) commonly abstracts graph-based and cluster-based ANNS as progressive SSD I/O that refines an in-flight candidate queue. It prefetches content for stable leading candidates under a bounded I/O budget, overlapping content reads with search without changing the final top-K results. Co-Retrieval-Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG) uses query logs to place frequently co-retrieved documents in contiguous segments. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) adapts this layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget. Group Content Fetch (GCF) exploits this layout to coalesce per-document random reads into batched, page-aware I/O requests. SICP works independently of the content layout, while RPAG and GCF reduce fetch cost even without prefetching.
  Across three multi-hop QA workloads with K from 10 to 1600, ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency over the best per-document-read baseline by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN. Separate experiments on 100M- and billion-vector indexes demonstrate SICP's applicability at larger scales.

title: Reflective Compositional Grounding for Natural-Language-to-SPARQL
summary: Natural-language query generation over large knowledge graphs embodies the classical vocabulary problem in human-systems communication. Questions express concepts through wording and compositions that can differ substantially from the target schema, while limited model context requires selective access to schema information. We present an NL2SPARQL framework that places conceptual compositionality at the center of query interpretation and connects it to the relational composition required for binding and query construction. A fixed concept encoder represents compound expressions jointly, and schema candidates are ranked using semantic similarity, type compatibility, and hierarchy proximity. Reflective refinement critically examines how the grounded meanings are realized through argument bindings, joins, and operator scope. Diagnosed semantic discrepancies guide revisions to the responsible stage. We formalise a monotone refinement discipline that accumulates scoped interpretation requirements and establish conditions under which changes to the composed process preserve previously validated interpretations. Across five benchmark/knowledge-graph targets, mean schema recall@10 increases from 0.712 to 0.837. With retrieval held fixed, reflective prompt rewriting adds 2.27-3.33 answer-F1 points. These experiments evaluate the grounding and refinement mechanisms, while the formal analysis specifies the stronger requirements for conservative adaptation across queries.

title: TraHist: Fast and Accurate Cardinality Estimation for Trajectory Data (Extended Version)
comment: Extended version of the paper to appear in PACMMOD Vol. 4, No. 6 (SIGMOD 2027)
summary: Cardinality estimation is fundamental for query optimization in database systems. Histogram-based estimators are widely used for their simplicity and efficiency but rely on point-centric partitioning that assumes record independence. This assumption breaks in trajectory data, where records from the same moving object show strong spatiotemporal dependencies. Conventional axis-aligned histograms therefore fragment trajectories across partition boundaries, leading to overestimation through duplicate counting. This error reflects a structural limitation of partition boundaries that are misaligned with trajectory-induced density patterns. To this end, we propose TraHist, a histogram-based estimator approximating density-aligned partitioning via efficient grid-based propagation. TraHist builds density-adaptive rectilinear buckets to preserve trajectory continuity and local density coherence while keeping histogram efficiency. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets show that TraHist reduces estimation error by over 20x relative to the strongest competing estimator in query regimes where trajectory fragmentation is a dominant source of estimation error, while maintaining sub-millisecond query latency and competitive construction cost.

title: Machine Learning-based Query Performance Optimization in Large-Scale IoT Databases
summary: The rapid growth of Internet of Things (IoT) deployments generates continuous, high-volume telemetry that strains query processing in large-scale databases, and static rule-based or cost-based optimizers do not adapt to the resulting workload variability. This research proposes a machine learning-based query performance optimization framework that identifies high-priority telemetry records from predicted operating conditions and formalizes a mathematically defined priority-scoring mechanism that a database system can use to allocate indexing, caching, and execution resources adaptively. The framework was developed and validated using the publicly available Environmental Sensor Telemetry Data set (405,184 raw IoT records collected over eight days from three Raspberry Pi-based sensor nodes; cleaned to 385,452 records), with a binary hazard label derived from carbon-monoxide (CO) concentration against an EPA-informed threshold. Seven candidate classifiers, K-Nearest Neighbors, Logistic Regression, an Artificial Neural Network, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Linear Discriminant Analysis, a Support Vector Machine, and CatBoost, were trained on a stratified-representative 10,000-record sample (8,000 train / 2,000 test, class balance within 0.5 percentage points of the full population) and compared on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-measure, prediction variance, and mean absolute error. CatBoost was selected as the proposed model, achieving 99.9% accuracy (95% CI: 99.76–100.00%), compared with 92.1–95.0% for the next-best classifiers. A correlation analysis quantified strong collinearity among CO, LPG, and smoke channels (r 1.00) and a moderate negative association with humidity (r 0.70 to 0.71), which is shown to reduce the effective dimensionality of the sensor feature space and motivates a composite-index recommendation for the underlying time-series store. The trained classifier's output probability is used to define a formal query/index priority score and a resource-allocation objective for adaptive optimization. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a statistically validated, computationally efficient basis for adaptive IoT query optimization; full deployment-scale latency benchmarking against a live database engine is identified as future work.

title: IEO-IM: influence maximization in social networks using improved equilibrium optimizer
summary: Influence maximization (IM) is a central problem in social network analysis. It aims to identify a small set of users capable of maximizing information diffusion across the network. Since IM is an NP-hard problem, many existing approaches depend on greedy or sampling-based techniques. However, these methods often face scalability challenges when applied to large networks. In this paper, an Improved Equilibrium Optimizer for Influence Maximization (IEO-IM) framework is presented. This method extends the Equilibrium Optimizer through a sequence of progressively refined strategies. The framework progressively improves search guidance, population diversity, and adaptive refinement. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated on six real-world social network datasets: Facebook, Epinions, YouTube, NetScience, High Energy Physics-Phenomenology (HEP-PH), and High Energy Physics-Theory (HEP-TH). They are assessed under the Independent Cascade (IC) model. Influence spread is estimated using Reverse-Reachable (RR) sets during optimization. It is also independently evaluated through Monte Carlo (MC) simulations for final evaluation. The framework comprises three incremental variants, denoted IEO1, IEO2, and IEO3. IEO1 incorporates two-hop influence-aware search guidance, IEO2 adds population clustering, and IEO3 incorporates rank-adaptive learning. Experimental results show that IEO3 generally achieves higher or comparable influence spread across most datasets, with improvements varying according to the network and seed size. Statistical analysis shows significant gains over most competitors, while the closest methods remain comparable. The framework also shows competitive computational performance on the evaluated networks, including the large-scale YouTube network. From a high-performance computing perspective, the IEO-IM workflow involves repeated RR-based fitness evaluations, population-based optimization, and Monte Carlo simulations, and its task-level multicore execution is evaluated experimentally across independent runs. On the Epinions network, eight worker processes reduce the median wall-clock time by approximately 72.0% compared with single-worker execution, corresponding to a speedup. A complete single-worker execution is also demonstrated on the million-node YouTube network.

title: AGRL: An Agentic GraphRAG Framework with Reinforcement Learning for Database Configuration Debugging
summary: Database configuration debugging aims to identify suitable parameter (knob) settings to resolve performance or stability issues. This task remains challenging even for experts due to the complexity and interdependencies of modern database settings. Recent work has explored vector-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to assist large language models (LLMs) in automatic configuration debugging by retrieving relevant database knowledge. However, this approach relies solely on surface-level semantic similarity, missing the deeper conceptual relationships essential for root cause diagnosis, which limits its effectiveness. To overcome this, we propose AGRL, an agentic GraphRAG framework empowered by reinforcement learning for database configuration debugging. AGRL has two core designs. First, a synergistic component co-design integrates: (1) a hybrid graph constructor utilizing historical Q&A pairs as semantic bridges to enrich database manuals; (2) a reinforced graph retriever featuring a mixture-of-experts (MoE) encoder and a dual-stage decision mechanism to extract precise subgraphs; and (3) a multi-round debugging agent that decomposes queries and performs an iterative ''Reason-Act-Reflect'' workflow while regulating retrieval breadth and depth. Second, AGRL employs a progressive training strategy, which combines decoupled initialization with iterative joint refinement, to overcome the cold-start interdependency between the agent and the retriever. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that AGRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods.

title: Fast Trajectory Similarity Computation over Road networks
summary: With the widespread application of trajectory data in areas such as traffic management and route planning, efficiently computing trajectory similarity for fast retrieval has become a critical challenge. Existing methods for trajectory similarity measurement often face issues of low computational efficiency and poor scalability when dealing with spatiotemporal constraints and complex structural correlations in the data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Highly Efficient Graph-based Recurrent Unit (HGRU) method for fast trajectory retrieval over road networks. The model connects nodes based on logical associations rather than restricting connections to physical adjacencies. Furthermore, a novel sample construction strategy is introduced, leveraging node adjacency relationships in real trajectory activities to create positive sample trajectories, while generating random non-adjacent negative sample trajectories to enhance model discrimination capability. Then with the help of efficient edge indexing techniques, the node features of the point-fusion graph are processed through a multi-head attention-enhanced graph convolutional network to capture topological information among nodes and construct trajectory embeddings. Subsequently, these trajectory embeddings are processed by a multi-layer gated recurrent unit network, which extracts and integrates deep spatiotemporal features to generate embeddings that accurately represent trajectory similarity. Experimental results on the T-drive and New York datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in trajectory similarity measurement, achieving higher efficiency and accuracy, especially when dealing with incomplete and structurally complex trajectory data, showing exceptional robustness.

title: Optimization, Modeling, and Integration in Intelligent Database Systems
summary:
Database systems and artificial intelligence are increasingly evolving toward a closely connected technical landscape. On the one hand, modern database systems must support increasingly complex workloads, heterogeneous data, and intelligent applications. On the other hand, recent advances in machine learning, reinforcement learning, generative models, and large language models have created new opportunities for improving database systems at multiple levels. This thesis investigates how artificial intelligence can support building intelligent database systems from three complementary perspectives: optimization, modeling, and integration.
First, this thesis studies learning-based query optimization, with a focus on join order selection and learned query optimizers. It reviews the current landscape of deep reinforcement learning-based methods and further explores a generative perspective for learned query optimization through adversarial plan generation. Second, this thesis investigates relational schema generation for multi-model data. It summarizes existing methods for mapping semi-structured data and graph data into relational form, and then studies reinforcement learning as a workload-aware approach for generating relational schemas automatically. Third, the thesis examines the integration of databases and large language models in industrial and business applications. It analyzes representative integration strategies and discusses their major trade-offs and open challenges.

title: SQL Query Optimization Through AI Agents
summary: Query optimization is crucial for modern data-driven applications and decision support systems to achieve accurate and timely results. SQL (Structured Query Language) still represents the primary user interface for relational databases; however, due to growing data volume, highly complex workloads, and hardware capacity expansion, traditional rule-based and cost-based query optimizers cannot handle these dynamic environments, as they are reliant upon fixed heuristics and pre-computed statistics that cannot adapt to real-time conditions. Therefore leading to a degradation in performance over time. This paper present an AI Agent-based hybrid framework to autonomously analyze SQL queries, estimate plans using closed-loop feedback mechanisms, including reinforcement learning (RL) and a genetic algorithm (GA). The framework has been implemented against PostgreSQL using a real world retail transactional dataset from Kaggle. Through rigorous experimentation, the results reveal that both GA and RL reducers outperform the built-in database optimizer, particularly for larger sets of complex multi-join and aggregation statements than most traditional query optimization tools/approaches can handle in an enterprise resource consumption when using this intelligent, self-learning system.

title: From GPU Cost Characterization to Memory-Aware Query Execution in Sirius
summary: GPU query performance depends on how an engine represents, moves and reuses data as well as on the kernels that execute its operators. This paper investigates these decisions in Sirius, a GPU-native SQL engine integrated with DuckDB. We begin with a question: which cost information is sufficient to choose a useful execution strategy? A standalone calibration shows that logical byte counts and a simple address-sector estimate fail to predict latency reliably, motivating a cost representation that includes access pattern, placement and reuse. We then evaluate three execution alternatives in Sirius: smaller scan batches, reader-side filter just-in-time compilation, and decoded GPU residency. The first two alternatives fail to improve the tested query. Keeping a fixed column union resident on the GPU improves complete hot query latency on two fixed TPC-H SF1 queries: independent paired measurements give speed ratios of 3.23 for Q6 and 1.73 for Q1. Residency incurs an upfront pin cost of approximately 64 ms, making reuse central to the decision. These results support placement-aware optimization on this workload and identify the measurements needed for an automatic GPU cost model. They do not establish a general cost predictor or a benefit from new kernel fusion.

title: JetStream: Generating Verified Query Accelerators for Existing Database Systems
summary: Recent work has shown that LLMs can synthesize highly specialized database systems for fixed workloads, but these systems replace the DBMS's native storage and assume static data: users must migrate their data, often give up ad-hoc queries, and lose acceleration once the data changes. We present JetStream, which instead generates query-specific accelerators that extend an existing DBMS. Given a set of parametrized query templates, a staged agentic workflow synthesizes accelerators that run directly over the DBMS's native tables and may maintain custom auxiliary state, while the DBMS remains responsible for storage, transactions, recovery, and all other queries. A fixed, engine-neutral substrate handles engine-specific hooks and keeps auxiliary state transactionally consistent under writes. JetStream generates two kinds of accelerators: tested accelerators, which may use any optimization and are validated by differential testing, and verified accelerators which trade some performance for a machine-checked proof that every answer satisfies a trusted specification derived from the SQL. On TPC-H at SF=20, JetStream achieves a geomean read speedup over DuckDB ( verified) and retains under a continuous update stream of 10,000 modified rows per second.

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
summary: Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: PFedMA: Who Should Join Next as Federated Multi-Agent Orchestration Evolves?
summary: Federated Multi-Agent Systems (FedMAS) offer a promising paradigm for collaborative reasoning among LLM-based agents while keeping raw client data decentralized. However, reliable multi-round collaboration remains challenging. Agent selection must take into consideration evolving task requirements and the agent's historical reliability, while privacy rules must adapt to changing collaboration contexts and meet the client's personalized needs. To address these challenges, we propose PFedMA, a federated multi-agent framework for feedback driven multi-round collaboration under heterogeneous privacy requirements. Across rounds, PFedMA maintains historical capability and reliability states to guide agent selection, evaluates task responses before aggregation, and refines subsequent queries according to accumulated collaboration feedback. PFedMA enables bidirectional local to global and global to local private rule evolution across heterogeneous clients. Clients generalize locally updated privacy rules and selectively incorporate globally maintained rules, thereby facilitating cross-client privacy rule evolution while preserving personalized constraints. Extensive experiments across reasoning, privacy sensitive, and adversarial settings show that PFedMA improves task performance, reduces measured privacy leakage, and improves system robustness.

title: Green Offloading and Model Size Adaptation for Federated Learning in IoT and Next-Generation Networks
summary: Federated learning (FL) trains models across geographically dispersed clients whose electricity carries very different carbon intensities. We present FedGreenCS, a carbon-aware approach to FL for IoT and next-generation networks. Clients are first grouped by data distribution similarity, using pairwise cosine similarity of model weights after a single local epoch. In each subsequent round, a sampled client whose carbon intensity exceeds a fixed tolerance offloads its training to the lowest-carbon available peer in its similarity cluster, while clients within the tolerance participate unchanged. Ordered dropout gives clients with a higher carbon intensity a narrower model. We derive a carbon cost model that separates computation and communication for each client and round, isolates the cost of the mandatory first-round broadcast, and states the design over the scaling rates and the tolerance. On a non-IID EMNIST partition with real regional carbon intensities, FedGreenCS with three carbon clusters reaches 70% test accuracy at 3.15 to 3.36 g CO2 of client-side carbon cost over three seeds, against 3.58 g for FedGreen and 15.12 g for FedAvg. With one model width for all clients, the offloading cuts this cost by 23% to 58%, but it raises the cost with two carbon clusters and always needs more rounds.

title: Frozen History: When Temporal Losses Stop Accumulation in Learned Real-Time Supersampling
summary: Learned real-time supersampling accumulates jittered low-resolution samples along motion vectors. Many methods use a temporal consistency loss to reduce flicker. We show that with accurate registration, this loss can suppress accumulation: on static content, the network copies its warped history at almost no temporal cost. Camera jitter in motion vectors raises this cost and can hide the effect. We identify four registration errors that training can conceal: jitter-carrying motion vectors, one motion field for both resolution lattices, jittered depth, and an unregistered skip path. A model-free oracle shows that correct registration makes freezing two orders of magnitude cheaper on static pixels. Controlled training shows that registration reverses the temporal weight's effect on PSNR. Under exact registration, increasing the weight reduces pixel variance at the expense of accuracy and perceived quality, with a 0.7 to 0.9 dB loss on static frames at weight 0.25. This reversal recurs across three network families and two scales; the loss also reduces accuracy on unjittered STSS data. With a small temporal weight and a normalised sample accumulator, a plain registered network improves the best published QRISP PSNR by 0.34 to 0.62 dB at 2, 3 and 4 upscaling to 1080p. At 2, its static pixel standard deviation is one quarter that of DLSS 2. Without retraining, it outperforms classical temporal upsampling by at least 4.4 dB on Arm's jittered Bistro capture. Our most accurate 4 model runs in 2.03 ms per 1080p frame on an H200. Code: https://github.com/CV-AC/Frozen_history

title: On the operational challenges of federated learning: sustainability, cost efficiency, and regulatory compliance in multicloud infrastructures
summary: Federated Learning has emerged as a transformative paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative model training, enabling geographically distributed institutions to build shared intelligence without ever exposing their local data. Its appeal is particularly strong in regulated domains such as healthcare and finance, where data sovereignty and legal accountability are non-negotiable. Yet as FL matures from research prototype to production infrastructure, a deeper challenge surfaces: real-world deployments increasingly span multiple cloud providers simultaneously, introducing a layer of operational complexity that existing frameworks are not equipped to handle. Managing heterogeneous billing models, fragmented resource telemetry, and provider-specific APIs across AWS, Azure, and GCP creates inefficiencies that translate directly into financial waste, unnecessary carbon emissions, and reduced organizational control, undermining the very sustainability goals that motivate cloud-native AI adoption. Beyond cost and sustainability, regulated FL deployments face an equally critical gap at the compliance layer. Collaborating across institutional and national boundaries requires demonstrable adherence to data protection regulations, contractual obligations, and runtime integrity standards, requirements that current orchestration solutions largely ignore. The result is a fragmented landscape where privacy-preserving algorithms coexist with legally unverifiable infrastructure, audit trails are incomplete or absent, and the environmental cost of distributed training remains invisible and unmanaged. Addressing these gaps in isolation is insufficient; what is needed is a unified approach that treats financial sustainability, environmental responsibility, and regulatory compliance as inseparable, co-equal objectives of the orchestration layer itself. This thesis presents two novel, complementary contributions that jointly address these open problems. The first, ECOFED, tackles the multicloud sustainability challenge by introducing a FinOps-driven orchestration middleware that brings financial observability and dynamic resource governance to federated training workloads. By treating environmental sustainability as a direct consequence of sound financial management, minimizing idle cloud resources reduces both cost and carbon footprint simultaneously, allowing the framework to enable organizations to run FL pipelines across heterogeneous providers in a way that is both economically viable and ecologically responsible. The second contribution, ECOFED-X, builds on this foundation by adding a compliance-aware, zero-trust orchestration layer designed for safety-critical applications. It ensures that participation in each training round is governed by verifiable legal, contractual, and runtime conditions, and that every decision is permanently recorded for regulatory auditability without ever centralizing sensitive data. Taken together, these contributions represent a novel and holistic step forward for Federated Learning infrastructure: from a model-centric paradigm operating in isolated cloud silos, toward a governance-aware, sustainability-driven, and legally accountable system capable of meeting the demands of modern regulated environments. Experimental validation in realistic multicloud scenarios confirms that strong operational and compliance guarantees can be achieved with negligible impact on model quality, positioning this work as a concrete path toward responsible, scalable, and green federated learning.

title: Learning based Scalable Multi-Objective Scheduling of Workflows across UD-IaaS-FaaS Systems
summary: Workflow scheduling in user device-centric edge-cloud computing has emerged as a challenging problem due to the need to jointly optimize execution performance, energy consumption, and monetary cost. Modern workflows consist of heterogeneous tasks, where compute-intensive components are well-suited for Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) resources, while fine-grained, event-driven tasks are more efficiently executed using the Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) model. We formulate this scheduling problem for application workflows over a hybrid User Device (UD)-IaaS-FaaS computing continuum as a multi-objective Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). The formulation models the workflow execution mechanism by incorporating cumulative capacity constraints for IaaS resources and elastic resource provisioning for FaaS. To overcome the intractability of MILP, we propose a learning-based framework that combines graph neural networks, surrogate performance modeling, and a multi-sample REINFORCE approach. The proposed approach is workflow-aware, leveraging task pairing to improve data locality and structured task placement decisions. Agent training is organized into three stages: small-scale learning of UD-IaaS trade-offs, intermediate locality aware co-location, and large-scale handling of parallelism and aggregation bottlenecks in workflows. The proposed framework is validated through real-world experiments using the Pegasus Montage workflow on a custom UD-IaaS-FaaS testbed comprising a user device, multiple IaaS nodes, and serverless FaaS instances. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the improved trade-offs across makespan, energy consumption, and cost. Compared with the genetic algorithm and greedy scheduling approaches, the proposed approach reduces makespan by 10-17.5%, energy consumption by 3-9%, and cost by 4-10%, while remaining within 3.5-5.6% of the MILP optimum.

title: Resource-Aware Quantum Big Data Analytics: A Hybrid Quantum–Classical Framework And Scalability Study For Post-Exascale Systems
summary: Quantum processors are often proposed as accelerators for data-intensive analytics, yet the cost of loading classical data, repeating circuits, and reading out measurements is rarely included when such proposals are assessed. This paper presents Q-BDA, a five-layer framework that places a quantum subroutine inside a hybrid pipeline and judges it with an end-to-end cost model covering encoding, circuit execution, shot sampling, communication, and classical post-processing. The framework is tested with a fidelity quantum kernel built from a two-repetition ZZ feature map and simulated exactly, without noise, on a single CPU core. Over ten random splits, the quantum-kernel support-vector machine reached 94.5%, 98.7% and 92.5% test accuracy on the Moons, Circles and Breast Cancer data, against 97.2%, 99.5% and 94.2% for a tuned RBF kernel. A kernel build needs one circuit per matrix entry, 291,480 circuits at N= 800, and explicit pairwise simulation was 84 times slower than a statevector shortcut that has no hardware counterpart. When the number of qubits grew from 2 to 12, off-diagonal kernel values fell from 0.39 to 0.0009, test accuracy on Breast Cancer fell from 94% to 73% while the RBF baseline stayed above 94%, and the shots needed to resolve a typical kernel value rose from 1.6 to 1,200. A parametric projection suggests that direct kernel construction for 10 4 samples would occupy a superconducting-type device for roughly nine days to five months. The results support treating quantum hardware as a workload-selective accelerator, and they provide a reproducible protocol for deciding when it is worth using.

title: Explainable Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving Cyberattack Detection and Resilient Energy Management in Distributed Smart Grids
summary: Distributed smart grids (feeders, microgrids and substations operated by different parties) generate the telemetry that could train cyberattack detectors, but the parties cannot pool it: it reveals customers and operations, and regulation forbids its transfer. Federated learning (FL) trains a shared detector without moving the data, differential privacy bounds what the shared model reveals, and explainable AI (XAI) tells an operator why an alarm was raised, which an energy-management system must know before it acts. This article designs a data-driven analytics framework that joins the three and evaluates it on a transparent simulation testbed: twelve heterogeneous grid clients; five attack classes (false-data injection, replay, denial of service, scaling and command injection) injected into 15-minute telemetry windows; and six training schemes (local, centralised, FedAvg, FedProx, FedAvg with record-level differential privacy, and robust aggregation under model-poisoning clients). On each client's own attack mix the schemes were within 0.03 AUROC of one another and local models were as good as any; on attacks a client had not seen, the federated and central detectors held their quality (AUROC 0.87–0.88) while local models fell to 0.74, with FedProx the better federated scheme under heterogeneity. Record-level differential privacy at single-digit ε erased all but the strongest attack signature with 700 windows per client; one poisoning client in twelve destroyed plain averaging while the coordinate-wise median withstood three. At cost-tuned thresholds federation saved 3.3 thousand per client-year over local detection on unseen attacks (positive in 71% of economic draws) and lost 6.6 thousand on seen ones; the attack rate and damage drive the value, poisoners and privacy noise reverse it. Shapley explanations of the federated and centralised detectors agree (rank correlation 0.72–0.79) and a four-rule surrogate reproduces 96% of the federated detector's decisions. All inputs are stylised with stated ranges; the testbed and results file accompany the article.

title: From Human Corrections to Learned Segmentations: A Critical Mathematical Review of Information, Learning, and Human Effort
summary: When does a human correction become useful learning, and what establishes better segmentation at matched human effort? This critical narrative review follows feedback through its selection, learner update, and evaluation. It compares active learning, machine teaching, interactive segmentation, and sequential predictive evaluation using a common mathematical account of target information, predictive error, response predictability, and human work. An exact Bayesian update converts evaluation-label information into expected log-loss improvement; an excess-risk decomposition explains what an approximate learner can lose. Conditional information decompositions separate the roles of selected locations, labels, and displayed context. Empirical comparisons show why response protocols, update mechanisms, and effort denominators matter, distinguishing current-mask refinement from reusable learning and simulated interaction from human evidence. We identify what logs can reveal, what requires independent evaluation, and what remains model-dependent. The resulting research priorities are to test what selection reveals, whether using it improves assimilation, and whether the resulting interaction policy benefits segmentation at matched effort. These are distinct claims: predicting a teacher's responses need not identify human intentions or establish better learning. No new acquisition algorithm or empirical superiority is claimed.

title: AI-Assisted Human Oversight in Credit-Card Fraud Detection: A Comparative Evaluation of Review-Routing Strategies under Analyst-Capacity Constraints
summary: This paper compares three routing strategies that decide which credit-card transactions an AI system resolves automatically and which it escalates to a human fraud analyst under a fixed review-capacity budget. Using XGBoost as a shared baseline classifier on the ULB Credit Card Fraud dataset (284,807 transactions, 492 frauds), we evaluate confidence-ranked review, two-dimensional risk-confidence routing, and an uncertainty-based deferral surrogate across review capacities from 0.5% to 20% of the test set. With an analyst modeled at 0.8 sensitivity, the confidence-ranked router reaches 71.1% recall at 5% capacity, while the risk-confidence and uncertainty routers reach only 23.7% and 23.0%; the gap widens as capacity shrinks. This ordering is unchanged when the analyst's sensitivity is varied from 0.6 to 0.9; the confidence-ranked router remains dominant and all strategies lose recall as the analyst weakens. The comparison depends on the metric: under equal-count recall, transaction amount dilutes confidence, but under amount-weighted loss, the two-dimensional router recovers 76.1% of fraudulent exposure versus 71.9%. At 20% capacity, the confidence router reaches 78.5% recall, exceeding the 75.9% of a fixed-threshold pure model and approaching the 80.0% of a pure human that reviews every case, with one-fifth of the human effort. Routing design materially changes fraud capture under a capacity constraint, and the value of a routing signal must be judged against the loss function an institution minimises. We translate these results into a risk-based human-oversight framework that matches the routing strategy to analyst capacity, transaction risk, and the institution's loss function.

title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.

title: Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning
summary: We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning. The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximises expected terminal utility with a running penalty on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of one-period losses. We estimate a conditional vine model from historical returns and use it to generate joint scenarios for CVaR evaluation and conditional paths for training a recurrent portfolio policy. Under uniform local derivative bounds, we propagate edgewise pair-copula parameter errors through the conditional transforms to obtain power-law stability bounds in Hellinger distance and total variation. In a finite-horizon investment model, we combine these estimates with a marginal and structural approximation budget to bound policy values, optimal values and the true-market loss of policies selected under a fitted model, with separate simulation and numerical optimisation terms. On a seven-asset panel comprising US and Chinese equities and gold, the selected ensemble of ten trained policies achieves a compound annual growth rate of 34.13% and a Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 complete monthly holding periods, exceeding the corresponding values of six classical and vine-based benchmarks. Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.
